course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 5
unit.description: Follow Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War, the sectional conflict over slavery, the election of 1860 and secession, the Civil War, and Reconstruction and its failure from 1844 to 1877.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a similarity between the Union and the Confederacy during the Civil War?
choices: Both relied on a large navy to blockade the ports of the other side
Both fought almost entirely on the territory of the Confederate states
Both used conscription and faced opposition to the draft at home
Both paid for the war entirely through taxes and avoided paper money
questions.explanation: The Confederacy passed a draft in 1862 and the Union in 1863, and both laws provoked protest.
choiceExplanations: Only the Union blockaded its enemy's ports.
Battles took place in the North as well.
The Confederacy passed a draft in 1862 and the Union in 1863, and both laws provoked protest.
Both governments printed paper money.
questions.distinguisher: The navy choice is close because both sides had ships, but the Union held the navy and used it to blockade the South.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: The New York City draft riots of July 1863 were a protest against
choices: a draft law that let men avoid service by paying $300 or hiring a substitute
a Confederate attack on New York harbor that threatened the city's trade
a tax on imported goods that had raised prices in the city's stores
a strike by factory workers who were seeking higher wages in the city's mills
questions.explanation: Many poor workers resented a law that allowed the wealthy to buy their way out of service, and the riot turned violent.
choiceExplanations: Many poor workers resented a law that allowed the wealthy to buy their way out of service, and the riot turned violent.
No such attack took place.
The riots concerned the draft.
The riots were a protest against the draft.
questions.distinguisher: The Confederate attack choice is close because the war made many Northerners fear for their cities, but the riot was a protest against the draft.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The Anaconda Plan proposed by General Winfield Scott called for the Union to
choices: invade the South in a single drive to capture Richmond at once
blockade Southern ports and take control of the Mississippi River
ask Britain to join a blockade of the Confederate coast
negotiate an end to the war after the first major Union victory
questions.explanation: The plan aimed to squeeze the Confederacy by closing its ports and splitting it along the Mississippi.
choiceExplanations: Scott's plan called for a long and slow squeeze.
The plan aimed to squeeze the Confederacy by closing its ports and splitting it along the Mississippi.
Britain was not asked to join.
The plan assumed a long war.
questions.distinguisher: The Richmond choice is close because the capture of Richmond was a Union goal, but the Anaconda Plan was a slow strategy of blockade and river control.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following helped the Union to defeat the Confederacy?
choices: A navy built by the Confederacy that could not be stopped by the Union
Recognition of the Union by Britain and France, who sent money and ships
The loyalty of all slave states, including Virginia, Tennessee, and Arkansas
Its greater population and its larger number of factories and railroads
questions.explanation: The North could put more soldiers in the field and could supply and move them more easily.
choiceExplanations: The Union held the navy and blockaded the South.
Neither power sent aid to the Union.
Those states joined the Confederacy.
The North could put more soldiers in the field and could supply and move them more easily.
questions.distinguisher: The Confederate navy choice is close because the Confederacy did use some ships and raiders, but it never broke the Union blockade.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The Union victories at Gettysburg and Vicksburg in July 1863 had which result?
choices: They forced the Confederacy to ask for peace within a few months
They caused Britain to recognize the Confederacy as an independent nation
They ended Lee's invasion of the North and gave the Union the Mississippi River
They led Lincoln to issue the Emancipation Proclamation to the Confederate states
questions.explanation: Gettysburg turned back Lee's army in Pennsylvania, and the fall of Vicksburg split the Confederacy.
choiceExplanations: The war lasted until 1865.
Britain never recognized the Confederacy.
Gettysburg turned back Lee's army in Pennsylvania, and the fall of Vicksburg split the Confederacy.
The Proclamation was issued on January 1, 1863.
questions.distinguisher: The peace within months choice is close because the victories changed the course of the war, but the fighting continued for nearly two more years.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a change in Union strategy by 1864?
choices: Attacking the railroads, farms, and cities of the South to break its ability to fight
Avoiding battle with Lee's army in order to preserve the Union's soldiers
Seeking a negotiated peace in which the Confederacy would keep its territory
Giving up the blockade of Southern ports in order to open trade with Britain
questions.explanation: Grant and Sherman moved from limited battles to a war on the South's resources, as in Sherman's march across Georgia.
choiceExplanations: Grant and Sherman moved from limited battles to a war on the South's resources, as in Sherman's march across Georgia.
Grant pressed Lee's army throughout 1864.
Lincoln insisted on reunion.
The blockade continued.
questions.distinguisher: The avoiding battle choice is close because Union commanders in the East had once been cautious, but Grant fought Lee continuously in 1864.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Sherman's capture of Atlanta in September 1864 contributed to Lincoln's re-election because
choices: it forced the Confederacy to surrender before the voters went to the polls
it raised Northern confidence that the Union would win the war
it ended the draft and allowed thousands of soldiers to return home to vote
it persuaded the Democrats to withdraw their candidate from the contest
questions.explanation: Before the victory many Northerners were tired of the war, and the fall of Atlanta renewed their hope of success.
choiceExplanations: The Confederacy surrendered in 1865.
Before the victory many Northerners were tired of the war, and the fall of Atlanta renewed their hope of success.
The draft continued.
The Democrats ran General McClellan.
questions.distinguisher: The surrender choice is close because Atlanta was a major blow, but the Confederate armies kept fighting until the spring of 1865.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The bread riots in Richmond in April 1863 are best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: The capture of the Confederate capital by Union troops in the spring of 1863
A dispute between farmers and merchants over the price of cotton in Britain
A strike by soldiers in the Confederate army who had not been paid in months
Shortages and rising prices in the South caused by the war and the blockade
questions.explanation: The war disrupted farming and trade, and the blockade and inflation made food scarce and costly.
choiceExplanations: Richmond did not fall until April 1865.
The riots concerned food in Richmond.
The rioters were civilians.
The war disrupted farming and trade, and the blockade and inflation made food scarce and costly.
questions.distinguisher: The capture of Richmond choice is close because the city was a target of the Union, but it was not captured until 1865.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the table?
choices: The Confederacy had more railroads than the Union but fewer people
The Union and the Confederacy were nearly equal in manufacturing
The Union had large advantages in population, railroads, and manufacturing
The Union's chief advantage was the large cotton crop that it grew and exported
questions.explanation: The table shows the Union with about 22 million people to the Confederacy's 9 million, more railroad mileage, and most of the nation's manufacturing.
choiceExplanations: The Union had more than twice as many miles of railroad.
The Union produced roughly nine-tenths of the nation's manufacturing.
The table shows the Union with about 22 million people to the Confederacy's 9 million, more railroad mileage, and most of the nation's manufacturing.
The Confederacy grew nearly all of the cotton.
questions.distinguisher: The railroads choice is close because the table does list railroad mileage, but it shows that the Union had more.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why the Confederacy's cotton did not bring it victory, despite its place in the table?
choices: Britain and France could buy all the cotton they needed from the Northern states
Confederate leaders refused to ship cotton to any foreign country during the war
The Confederacy had no way of growing cotton after the first year of the war
The Union's navy could blockade Southern ports and cut off the sale of cotton
questions.explanation: The table lists the Union as the holder of nearly all of the navy, which it used to close Southern ports.
choiceExplanations: The Northern states grew little cotton.
Southerners tried to sell cotton abroad.
Cotton continued to be grown.
The table lists the Union as the holder of nearly all of the navy, which it used to close Southern ports.
questions.distinguisher: The Northern states choice is close because Britain needed a supply of cotton, but the North grew little and could not replace the South.

questions.prompt: The differences shown in the table are best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: A federal program of the 1850s that had built factories in the Northern cities
Decades of Northern industrial growth and a Southern economy built on cotton and slavery
A Confederate decision in 1861 to stop building railroads in order to save money
A Union plan to destroy Southern factories during the first year of the war
questions.explanation: The North developed factories, railroads, and cities, while the South invested in land and enslaved laborers and exported cotton.
choiceExplanations: The government did not build the factories.
The North developed factories, railroads, and cities, while the South invested in land and enslaved laborers and exported cotton.
The differences existed before the war.
The Confederacy had few factories to destroy.
questions.distinguisher: The federal program choice is close because the government did support some economic growth, but private investors built the Northern factories.
